title: Drinkwel Review: Does the Multivitamin for Drinkers Work?
excerpt: An honest Drinkwel review: what's in the daily multivitamin for people who drink, how much DHM and NAC it can hold, side effects, interactions, and who it suits.
metaDescription: Honest Drinkwel review: ingredients, DHM and NAC doses, side effects, medication interactions, and whether a daily multivitamin for drinkers is worth it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Drinkwel is a capsule supplement sold as a daily multivitamin for people who drink. Instead of a pill you only take on a night out, it is built around a once-a-day routine that combines ordinary vitamins and minerals with ingredients linked to alcohol metabolism, such as DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree), NAC (N-acetyl cysteine, an amino acid your body uses to make the antioxidant glutathione), and milk thistle. That idea makes some sense, because regular drinking can wear down certain nutrients. But there is no large independent trial of Drinkwel itself, there is no good evidence that taking it every day prevents hangovers, and the daily habit means you take more pills, for longer, than you would with a product you only use on drinking nights.

**Who it suits:** people who drink a few times a week, already like taking a daily multivitamin, and want one product that covers both. **Who should skip it:** people who drink only now and then (a daily product mostly gets taken on days you don't drink), people who mainly want DHM (a plain DHM product gives you more per serving and per dollar), and people on several prescription medicines, because a long daily ingredient list raises more interaction questions.

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains published research, the brand's own descriptions, and general supplement science. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Drinkwel is a dietary supplement, not a drug. It has not been approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and it does not lower your blood alcohol, sober you up, or make it safe to drive. **Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking it if** you take prescription medicine (especially blood thinners, diabetes medicines, nitroglycerin or other nitrates, sedatives, sleep aids, or anxiety medication), are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver or kidney disease. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken up, call 911.

**About our relationship with Drinkwel:** we don't have an affiliate arrangement with Drinkwel, so this review doesn't link to their store and we earn nothing if you buy it. We do earn a commission on two plain DHM products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## What Drinkwel Is

Drinkwel is a US supplement brand whose main product is a capsule it describes as a multivitamin for people who drink. The pitch is different from most hangover products. Brands like Flyby, Cheers, and AfterDrink are mostly built to be taken around a night of drinking. Drinkwel's marketing instead frames the product as something you take daily, the same way you'd take any other multivitamin, so that your body is "topped up" on the nutrients drinking tends to use up.

That positioning matters for how you judge it. A night-of product is judged on one question: do I feel better the next morning? A daily product asks you to believe something harder to test: that taking pills every day, including days you don't drink, adds up to a benefit over time. That is a bigger claim, and it is the claim with the least direct evidence behind it.

The brand has also changed its packaging, wording, and formula details over the years, which is common for small supplement brands. Older listings and reviews may describe a version that differs from what is sold today. Anything we say about ingredients below is based on how the product has generally been described, and you should check the label on the bottle in front of you before relying on it.

## Drinkwel Ingredients: What's in It and Why

Drinkwel's formula has generally combined three groups of ingredients. Here is what each group is there to do, and how strong the reasoning behind it is.

### 1. A standard multivitamin base

The foundation is the kind of vitamins and minerals you'd find in most multivitamins, with an emphasis on the ones alcohol is known to affect:

- **B vitamins**, especially thiamine (B1), along with B6, B12, folate, and others. Heavy, long-term drinking is a well-known cause of thiamine deficiency, which in severe cases can damage the brain and nerves. That's the strongest scientific reason for B vitamins in any drinker's formula. For a social drinker who eats a normal diet, the benefit is much less certain.
- **Vitamin C and other antioxidant vitamins**, pitched as helping with the oxidative stress (wear and tear on cells from reactive molecules) that breaking down alcohol creates.
- **Minerals such as zinc and magnesium.** Alcohol makes you urinate more, and heavy drinkers often run low on zinc and magnesium. Zinc is also used by the enzyme that does the first step of alcohol breakdown in your liver.

### 2. Alcohol-metabolism and liver ingredients

This is the part that makes Drinkwel a "drinker's" multivitamin rather than a regular one:

- **DHM.** The best-known hangover-supplement ingredient. In a widely cited 2012 rat study published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on the brain's GABA receptors (the same calming system alcohol acts on). Other lab and animal work suggests it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol that's linked to hangover symptoms. Human evidence is limited. A 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease found improvements in some liver markers, but that wasn't a hangover study.
- **NAC (N-acetyl cysteine).** NAC is the raw material your body uses to make glutathione, one of its main antioxidants. Hospitals give IV NAC as the antidote for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose for exactly this reason. Whether a daily NAC pill helps a healthy social drinker is much less clear, and human hangover research on it is thin. We compare the two in [NAC vs DHM](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025).
- **Milk thistle (silymarin).** The most studied liver herb. Human results for liver conditions are mixed, and there's no good evidence it prevents hangovers. It's generally well tolerated. See [DHM vs milk thistle](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-milk-thistle-which-liver-supplement-more-effective-2025) for how they differ.

### 3. Supporting botanicals

Depending on the version, the formula has also listed smaller amounts of herbal or plant extracts commonly found in hangover and liver products. These usually appear in small amounts and have little or no direct human research for hangovers.

### The dose question

Here is the problem most reviews skip. A daily serving is usually a couple of capsules. Each capsule holds a limited amount of powder, roughly 500 to 800 mg depending on size. When that space has to fit a full multivitamin plus DHM, NAC, milk thistle, and extracts, something has to give, and it's usually the dose of each individual ingredient.

That doesn't make the product useless. Vitamins and minerals work at small doses (micrograms and milligrams). But the ingredients with the most hangover interest, DHM and NAC, are typically studied and sold at hundreds of milligrams each. Standalone DHM products commonly provide 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving. A crowded daily formula usually can't match that. Check the Supplement Facts panel: if DHM is listed inside a "proprietary blend" without its own amount, you can't know how much you're getting, which is a reason for caution in itself.

## Does Drinkwel Work?

The honest answer: it may help some people feel a bit better, but it isn't proven, and the specific daily-use claim is the hardest part to support.

Here's how the evidence breaks down:

**What's reasonable.** People who drink regularly really can run low on some B vitamins, zinc, and magnesium. If your diet is poor and you drink several times a week, a multivitamin that covers those gaps is a sensible, low-risk idea. That's true whether the label says "for people who drink" or not.

**What's plausible but not established.** DHM and NAC have biological reasons to think they might help, mostly from lab and animal work. Small human studies exist for some ingredients, but not for this formula, and not for daily use as a hangover strategy.

**What has no good evidence.** There is no good evidence that taking a multivitamin every day prevents hangovers, protects your liver from regular drinking, or lets you drink more with fewer consequences. No independent clinical trial of Drinkwel itself has been published, as far as we can find.

**What user reviews tell you.** Customer reviews of Drinkwel, like those for nearly every hangover product, are split. Some people say they feel noticeably better and more energetic. Others notice nothing. Reviews are worth reading for practical details (capsule size, stomach upset, shipping), but they can't tell you much about effectiveness. People who feel better tend to credit the pill, when the real difference may be that they drank less, ate more, or slept better that night.

A useful test if you try it: judge it over a few weeks of your normal drinking, not one dramatic night, and keep everything else (number of drinks, food, water, sleep) roughly the same. If you can't tell the difference, you have your answer.

## Daily Multivitamin vs Night-Of Hangover Pill

This is the real decision behind a Drinkwel purchase, so it's worth spelling out.

| | Daily "drinker's multivitamin" (Drinkwel's approach) | Night-of hangover supplement (Flyby, Cheers, plain DHM) |
|---|---|---|
| When you take it | Every day, drinking or not | Only on nights you drink |
| Best case | Covers nutrient gaps from regular drinking and a weak diet | Concentrates the hangover-related ingredients when they might matter |
| Pills per month | Around 60 if you take two a day | Only as many as your drinking nights need |
| DHM per serving | Usually lower, because the space is shared with vitamins | Usually higher, especially in single-ingredient DHM |
| Interaction exposure | Constant, every day | Occasional |
| Who it fits | People drinking several times a week who want a multivitamin anyway | Occasional and weekend drinkers |

For most social drinkers, the night-of approach fits better. If you drink once or twice a week, a daily product means most of your capsules go down on sober days, and you're paying for that. If you already take a regular multivitamin, adding Drinkwel likely doubles up many of the same vitamins, which is wasteful at best and, for a few nutrients, can push you toward the upper safe limit.

If you drink often enough that a daily product seems necessary, that's worth a moment of honest thought on its own. The most effective way to feel better is still to drink less, drink slower, and eat and hydrate properly. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Is It Safe to Take DHM and NAC Every Day?

Because Drinkwel is meant to be taken daily, the long-term safety of its ingredients matters more than it would for an occasional product.

- **Vitamins and minerals.** Generally safe at multivitamin doses. The risk is doubling up: if you also take a separate multivitamin, a B-complex, or zinc, check that your totals stay under the upper limits on the label. High-dose vitamin B6 taken for a long time has been linked to nerve problems, and too much zinc over time can lower copper levels.
- **DHM.** No serious safety signals have been reported at typical doses, but long-term human safety data are limited. We go through what's known in [can you take DHM every day](/never-hungover/can-you-take-dhm-every-day-long-term-guide-2025).
- **NAC.** Widely used and usually well tolerated. Possible side effects include nausea, stomach upset, and diarrhea. NAC may thin the blood slightly and can interact with nitroglycerin and some blood pressure medicines, so people on those should ask first. NAC has also had an unusual regulatory history in the US: around 2021, the FDA questioned whether it could legally be sold as a supplement because it was first approved as a drug, and some retailers pulled NAC products for a while. That's one reason some brands have changed or reworded their formulas.
- **Milk thistle.** Generally well tolerated. It can cause stomach upset and may affect how the liver processes some medicines, and people allergic to ragweed or related plants may react to it.

The practical takeaway: a daily multi-ingredient product isn't dangerous for most healthy people, but "daily" plus "many ingredients" is exactly the combination where checking with a pharmacist is worth five minutes, especially if you take any prescription medicine.

## Drinkwel Side Effects

Most people report no problems. When complaints do come up with this type of product, they're usually:

- **Stomach upset or nausea**, especially taken on an empty stomach. Taking it with breakfast or a meal usually helps.
- **Bright yellow urine.** This is harmless and comes from riboflavin (vitamin B2), which your body excretes when it has enough.
- **Flushing or tingling**, which can happen with niacin (vitamin B3) at higher doses.
- **Headache or loose stools** in a minority of people, as with many supplements.
- **Allergic reactions** to herbal ingredients, which are rare but more likely the more botanicals a formula contains.

Stop taking it and talk to a doctor if you get a rash, hives, swelling, trouble breathing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or ongoing stomach pain. Those aren't normal supplement side effects.

## Drinkwel and Medications

Check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting Drinkwel if you take:

- **Blood thinners** (warfarin, apixaban, and similar) or daily aspirin. Some ingredients, including NAC and certain herbs, may add to bleeding risk.
- **Diabetes medicines.** Several herbal ingredients common in liver and hangover formulas may affect blood sugar.
- **Nitroglycerin or other nitrates.** NAC can strengthen their effect and cause headache or low blood pressure.
- **Sedatives, sleep aids, or anxiety medication.** DHM acts on GABA receptors in the brain, the same system these drugs act on, so caution is sensible.
- **Medicines processed by liver enzymes**, which covers a long list of common prescriptions. Milk thistle and some other botanicals may change how fast those are broken down.

Bring the bottle or a photo of the Supplement Facts panel so they can see every ingredient. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers the most common questions in more detail.

## How to Take Drinkwel

Follow the directions on the label, since serving size and timing have varied between versions. In general, Drinkwel has been marketed as a daily supplement taken once a day with food, rather than only before or after drinking. A few practical tips:

- **Take it with a meal.** Multivitamins and NAC are both easier on the stomach with food.
- **Don't stack it with your regular multivitamin** unless a pharmacist has checked the totals.
- **Don't take extra on heavy nights.** More capsules won't offset more drinks, and you'll just raise your vitamin and herb intake.
- **Keep drinking the basics.** Water between drinks, food before and during, and sleep matter more than any capsule.

## Where to Buy Drinkwel (and What to Watch For)

Drinkwel has been sold through its own website and through online marketplaces. If you search for it, you'll find a lot of third-party reseller listings and thin "review" pages that mostly exist to send you to a store. A few cautions:

- **Buy from the brand or an authorized seller** where you can. Third-party marketplace listings can carry old stock, older formula versions, or near-expiry bottles.
- **Check the expiration date and the seal** when it arrives.
- **Compare the label to the listing.** If the Supplement Facts panel on the bottle doesn't match what the listing described, contact the seller.
- **Watch subscription terms.** Many daily supplements are sold by subscription. Make sure you know how to pause or cancel before you sign up.

We don't link to a store for Drinkwel because we have no arrangement with the brand, and we'd rather not send you to a reseller we can't vouch for.

## Drinkwel vs Other Hangover Supplements

How Drinkwel compares to products we've reviewed:

- **Drinkwel vs plain DHM.** Plain DHM gives you a much larger dose of the one ingredient with the most hangover research, usually for less money, and you only take it when you drink. Drinkwel gives you a multivitamin plus a smaller amount of DHM, every day. If DHM is what you're after, a single-ingredient product is the more direct choice. See our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for amounts.
- **Drinkwel vs AfterDrink.** Both are broad, many-ingredient formulas with DHM as one part. AfterDrink is aimed at drinking nights; Drinkwel is aimed at daily use. Our [AfterDrink review](/never-hungover/afterdrink-review) goes through the same dose trade-off.
- **Drinkwel vs ZBiotics.** ZBiotics is a different idea entirely: a probiotic drink engineered to break down acetaldehyde in the gut. It's taken before drinking, not daily. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) covers what the evidence does and doesn't show.
- **Drinkwel vs a regular multivitamin.** If you drink lightly and eat reasonably well, a standard multivitamin (or none at all) may cover the same nutrient ground for less. Our guide to [vitamins for hangovers](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) explains which ones have a real reason to be there.

For a wider look at what each ingredient category can and can't do, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## Pros and Cons

**Pros**

- Thoughtful idea: covers nutrients that regular drinking is known to deplete, especially B vitamins, zinc, and magnesium
- Combines a multivitamin with DHM, NAC, and milk thistle in one product
- Daily routine can be simpler than remembering a pill on nights out
- Ingredients are generally well tolerated at typical doses
- Some users report feeling better and more energetic

**Cons**

- No independent clinical trial of the finished product
- No good evidence that a daily multivitamin prevents hangovers
- DHM and NAC doses are usually lower than in standalone products because space is shared with vitamins
- Daily use means paying for capsules on days you don't drink
- Easy to double up if you already take a multivitamin
- More daily ingredients means more to check for medication interactions
- Formula details have changed over time, and reseller listings may not match the current version

## If You Mainly Want DHM

If what drew you to Drinkwel was the DHM, a single-ingredient DHM product is the simpler, more direct option, and you only take it on the nights you drink. DHM is promising but not proven. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone. It does not lower your blood alcohol or make heavy drinking safe.

If you want to try it, two options we've looked at closely are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). (We earn a commission if you buy through these links, at no cost to you.) Our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side.

## The Bottom Line

Drinkwel is built on a reasonable idea: people who drink regularly can run short on some nutrients, and a daily multivitamin can cover those gaps. It isn't a scam, and it isn't a proven hangover cure. The weak spots are that the product itself hasn't been independently tested, the ingredients with the most hangover interest are usually present at modest doses, and daily use only makes sense if you drink often enough to justify it.

If you drink a few times a week, don't already take a multivitamin, and like the convenience, it's a reasonable product to try. Read the label, check it with a pharmacist if you take medicine, and judge it over a few normal weeks. If you drink occasionally, a night-of product or plain DHM is likely the better fit. And whatever you take, the things that matter most are still the unglamorous ones: drinking less, drinking slower, eating, drinking water, and sleeping.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Drinkwel actually work?**

It may help some people feel a bit better, but it isn't proven. No independent clinical trial of Drinkwel itself has been published that we can find. Some of its ingredients, such as DHM, NAC, and B vitamins, have biological reasons to be there, mostly from lab, animal, or nutrient-deficiency research. There is no good evidence that taking a daily multivitamin prevents hangovers. User reviews are mixed. It does not lower your blood alcohol or make heavy drinking safe.

**What are the ingredients in Drinkwel?**

Drinkwel has generally combined a multivitamin base (B vitamins including thiamine, vitamin C, and minerals such as zinc and magnesium) with ingredients linked to alcohol metabolism and the liver, such as DHM, NAC, and milk thistle, plus smaller amounts of plant extracts. The formula has changed over time, so check the Supplement Facts panel on the bottle you buy for the current list and amounts.

**Is Drinkwel a multivitamin or a hangover pill?**

It's marketed as a daily multivitamin for people who drink, not as a pill you take only on a night out. That's the main difference from products like Flyby, Cheers, or plain DHM, which are taken around drinking. Because it's daily, you'll take it on sober days too, so it makes the most sense for people who drink several times a week and want a multivitamin anyway.

**How much DHM is in Drinkwel?**

The amount has varied between versions, so check the label. In general, a daily formula that also has to fit a full multivitamin, NAC, and milk thistle into a couple of capsules can't hold as much DHM as a standalone DHM product, which commonly provides 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving. If DHM is listed inside a proprietary blend without its own amount, you can't tell how much you're getting.

**Does Drinkwel have side effects?**

Most people report none. Possible side effects include stomach upset or nausea (taking it with food helps), harmless bright yellow urine from vitamin B2, flushing from niacin, and occasionally headache or loose stools. Herbal ingredients can rarely cause allergic reactions. Stop and see a doctor if you get a rash, swelling, trouble breathing, yellow skin or eyes, or ongoing stomach pain.

**Can I take Drinkwel with my regular multivitamin?**

It's usually better not to. Drinkwel already contains many of the same vitamins and minerals, so taking both can double your intake. For most nutrients that's just wasteful, but for a few, such as vitamin B6, zinc, and vitamin A, high long-term intake can cause problems. If you want to take both, ask a pharmacist to check the combined totals.

**Can I take Drinkwel with medication?**

Ask a doctor or pharmacist first. Drinkwel's ingredients can interact with some medicines: NAC with nitroglycerin and possibly blood thinners, DHM with sedatives and anxiety medicines (it acts on the same GABA system), and milk thistle and other herbs with drugs processed by liver enzymes or diabetes medicines. Bring the bottle or a photo of the label so they can see every ingredient.

**Is Drinkwel worth the money?**

It depends on how often you drink. If you drink several times a week, don't take another multivitamin, and like having one daily product, it can be a reasonable choice. If you drink occasionally, you'll pay for capsules you mostly take on sober days, and a night-of product or plain DHM is likely better value. Either way, how much you drink, how fast, whether you eat, and how well you sleep matter more than any supplement.
